sources.title: Google Pixel Watch 5 Sale: Its Lowest Price Yet (2026)
sources.text:
If you’ve been waiting for a good deal on Google’s latest smartwatch before you commit, you're in luck. The Google Pixel Watch 5 (the 41-mm model with Wi-Fi) is currently $300, down from $400, marking its lowest price yet. (The larger 45-mm model is also discounted, from $430 to $330.)
This early Black Friday sale means you don’t have to wait until the late-November holiday to score the worthwhile discount—and we recommend you don't. Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store are all offering the 25 percent off deal, but I don't know for how much longer. In other words, now is a great time to score this smartwatch for less.
A Record-Low Price
The Pixel Watch 5 is one of the best smartwatches available for Android users. It’s a refinement of an already brilliant wearable, with double the RAM and storage, plus an upgraded Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor that makes this edition 20 percent faster than its predecessor. The domed display is gorgeous, comfortable, and easy to read during workouts, and it provides meaningful upgrades for health and fitness tracking.
Beyond being able to track weights and reps, the new Strength Training experience includes a workout builder, audio cues, and rest times. You can build a custom routine in the Google Health app and have the watch guide you through each exercise, and incorporate Gemini AI by asking it to generate a workout based on a photo of your gym equipment. Speaking of Gemini, the Pixel Watch 5 supports certain offline tasks, such as starting a workout, which is nice if you like to leave your watch at home while you exercise.
Google’s new Health Guardian tools include features for monitoring insulin resistance trends, blood pressure trends, breathing emergencies (available only in select countries), and sleep breathing quality. The watch also retains useful features like ECG, skin temperature tracking, and loss-of-pulse detection. It comes with upgraded sleep tracking, too, with Google claiming 15 percent greater accuracy than the Pixel Watch 4.
Google estimates up to 40 hours of battery life, but mine only got to around 36 hours in testing before conking out. Fast charging is the real standout, though; just 15 minutes on the charger delivers up to 15 hours of use. If you’re like me and only remember to charge your watch 20 minutes before leaving the house, this is a lifesaver.
At its original $400 price, the Pixel Watch 5 is a pricey recommendation, especially since many of its software upgrades will also make their way to the previous generation. But at $300, it’s cheaper than the latest Apple Watch Series 12 and other high-end smartwatches. This is the lowest price I’ve seen for the Pixel Watch 5, so if you’ve been eyeing it, there’s little reason to wait for Black Friday.

sources.title: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents
sources.text:
There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.
“I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said.
Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.
DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September, a CLI agent introduced in July, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos. The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering.
The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.

sources.title: Basically no one is using AI agents for their DoorDash orders
sources.text:
As AI tools and agents have continued their march across all aspects of digital life, many companies are trying to use LLMs to improve the experience of purchasing goods and services on the Internet. Thus far, though, a vanishingly small number of people seem to be taking advantage of those capabilities, at least when it comes to using the popular food delivery app DoorDash with an outside AI agent.
In a third-quarter earnings call Thursday, DoorDash co-founder and CEO Tony Xu responded to an analyst question by noting that "AI agents are generating several hundred orders [on DoorDash] across the time that they've been up and running." In a marked understatement, Xu called this a "very low use case" for a company that handled just shy of 1 billion orders total in the third quarter of 2026 alone.
Speaking generally, Xu said he sees the potential for AI agents to be genuinely helpful for "long consideration purchases" and major decisions where agents would be "doing work on your behalf proactively in the background." However, Xu added, "when it comes to a task that's as simple as ordering food, we tend to see that come directly to DoorDash."

sources.title: Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, report says
sources.text:
Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.
The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the investment giant and anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude-maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.
Now, Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.
TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.
Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, wracking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors.
Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry.

sources.title: Apple confirms iOS 27.3 beta is coming next week with Apple Intelligence in China
sources.text:
Apple today took the unusual step of confirming when its next iOS developer beta is expected to arrive, as part of an announcement detailing the upcoming launch of Apple Intelligence in China. Here are the details.
A bit of context
In mid-July, Reuters reported that, following a lengthy back-and-forth with Chinese regulators and multiple delays, Apple Intelligence had finally cleared a major regulatory hurdle ahead of its long-awaited launch in the country.
Then, a couple of weeks ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple was planning to launch Apple Intelligence in China in December as part of iOS 27.3, although without Siri AI and other newer features.
The following day, China’s state-backed media outlet The Paper reported that Tim Cook had confirmed regulatory approval for the platform, with a test version expected before the end of October.
Then, just last Monday, Apple released iOS 27.2 and its counterparts, expanding Siri AI support to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. On the same day, the company announced that four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, would be supported by the end of the year.
However, while that announcement confirmed additional language support for Siri AI, it offered no updates on the rollout of Apple Intelligence in China, where Siri AI itself will remain unavailable for the time being.
While Apple typically releases the first beta of its next software update shortly after the previous version becomes available, iOS 27.3 has yet to materialize.
Now, as spotted by MacRumors, a press release published on Apple’s Chinese Newsroom website confirms that testing of Apple Intelligence in China will begin on November 4, as part of the next iOS developer beta.
Importantly, Apple has only confirmed November 4 as the start of Apple Intelligence testing in China, not necessarily the release date of iOS 27.3 beta 1 itself.
Apple Intelligence coming to China
In the press release, Apple confirms that users in China will get an improved Siri experience, including Type to Siri and the ability to access Alibaba’s Qwen for certain requests, but not Siri AI itself.
The Qwen integration will also extend to Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence. According to Apple, users will be able to ask questions about photos and documents, including PDFs and presentations, as well as generate original content from scratch through Writing Tools. Users will be able to access Qwen by signing into their accounts or using Sign in with Apple.
Other features included in the initial rollout are Live Translation in Messages, FaceTime, and Phone, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up in Photos, natural-language photo searches, priority notifications, notification summaries, and Smart Reply, among others.
Apple also noted that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.
The features will be available on the iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone 16 and later, iPhone Air, and iPhone Duo, with both Siri and the device language required to be set to either English or Simplified Chinese.
The company also confirmed that the features will become publicly available in December, with the official release of iOS 27.3.

clusters.title_hint: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals

sources.title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
sources.text:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.
Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.
Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.
The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies.
“As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”
Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.
At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI, a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther, a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS.
Nexus, a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument.
Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours.
The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula.
Next, the team is evaluating open models including NVIDIA Nemotron for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon.

The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules.

I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.
That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.”

But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity. That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice.
The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. Apple has launched a wave of major new products since John Ternus took over as CEO, and a new interview with Ternus reveals how this aligns very much with his primary focus.
John Ternus names ‘product’ as the chief thing he’s passionate about and focused on
Following Apple’s unveil of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR earlier this week, CEO John Ternus sat down for an interview with Steven Levy at WIRED.
Much of the ground covered is familiar territory, with Ternus repeating things he’s said before.
But a standout focus that Ternus emphasizes, echoed by quotes from some of his top executives, is his deep passion for one thing: product.
I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I’m super passionate about it.”
Top comment by Chris
I like John, and I like engineer CEOs, and I hope he has a successful tenure. But so far I'd say his focus has been:
"Less Product for More Money"

If Apple’s huge wave of product launches since Ternus took over as CEO wasn’t evidence enough, the messaging from this new interview is clear: Ternus is focused on product.

sources.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
sources.text:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.
Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.

sources.title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
sources.text:
Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by the global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk, third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”
“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that there had been what could be characterized as an incident.
The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.
“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”

Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.
Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”

sources.text:
Waymo will begin testing autonomous Toyota bZ4X vehicles in Japan next year as part of a broader partnership with the automaker to provide electric vehicles for robotaxi operations in international markets, including the U.K.
Under the partnership announced Friday, Toyota will manufacture the 2027 bZ4X vehicles and integrate Waymo’s self-driving system at its Takaoka factory in Japan. (The electric vehicle is now known as the bZ in the North American market.)
The autonomous bZ4X vehicles will initially be tested in Japan, where Waymo intends to eventually operate a robotaxi service. But the intent is to deploy these vehicles in other right-hand driving countries such as the U.K. Waymo has been testing its autonomous Jaguar I-Pace vehicles in London for months and plans to launch a robotaxi service there once it receives the necessary permits.
The announcement comes 18 months after Toyota and Waymo signed a preliminary agreement to explore the development and deployment of an autonomous vehicle platform. At the time, the agreement fell into the “let’s see what happens” category, with language vague enough to leave plenty of room for interpretation.
For now, the partnership looks more like a conventional vehicle supplier deal that helps Waymo fill specific regional needs while adding a new model to its robotaxi portfolio.
But the partnership could go beyond robotaxis. The companies said they will continue to look at bringing Waymo’s autonomous technology to personally owned Toyota vehicles.
Toyota and Waymo also announced plans to look at other future “initiatives” that would use “insights from Waymo’s real-world operations” to improve safety for other road users. What that might mean is unclear, although Hiroki Nakajima, executive vice president of Toyota and a board member, provided some clues.
“This collaboration will help scale that technology and bring it to customers in Japan and beyond through Waymo’s ride-hailing service, and in parallel, Toyota will continue to explore how integrating vehicles with traffic infrastructure can make those roads safer still,” he said in a statement.

Waymo and Toyota will soon start testing their robotaxis in Japan
The companies plan to deploy their autonomous bZ4X vehicles to other right-hand drive markets like the UK.
In April 2025, Toyota and Waymo entered a preliminary agreement to work together on robotaxis. Now, the companies have announced that they will start testing an autonomous fleet of Toyota bZ4X electric vehicles in Japan sometime in 2027. After Japan, they're planning to deploy the vehicles to the UK and other right-hand drive markets in the years that follow.
The bZ4X is Toyota's first modern mass-market electric vehicle based on the e-TNGA platform it developed with Subaru. Toyota will be manufacturing the bZ4X units it's deploying and testing with Waymo at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture. That's also where the automaker is assembling the vehicles and equipping them with Waymo's autonomous vehicle hardware.

How to Detect Financial Fraud Patterns
with Knowledge Graphs: A Production
Guide
sources.text:
Most anti-fraud architectures in enterprise payment workflows evaluate transactions in isolation.
When an invoice arrives, an automated rules engine checks it against static thresholds. It checks whether the dollar amount falls within normal limits, whether the vendor is on an approved vendor list, and whether the submitting IP address looks familiar. If the individual attributes look plausible, the payment clears.
The problem with this approach is structural. Sophisticated fraud schemes like money mule rings, circular invoicing loops, and vendor collision rarely produce transactions that alert individual thresholds. A shell company invoicing $4,800 to stay under a $5,000 dual sign-off threshold looks completely fine in isolation. But when 25 seemingly independent vendors all route disbursements to the same bank account, the coordinated pattern starts to become clear.
You won't find the warning in the attributes of an isolated transaction. It lives in the topology of the payment network.
In a relational database, tracing these multi-entity relationships requires recursive cell joins across tables of vendors, invoices, payments, and bank accounts. But as tables grow into millions of rows, deep path traversals quickly degrade query performance. Graph databases solve this by storing relationships as first-class, index-free adjacency pointers, turning multi-hop traversals into constant-time lookups.
In this tutorial, you'll explore the architecture of an end-to-end relational fraud detection pipeline built on Neo4j. You'll see how to model financial entities as a graph, precompute derived edges to optimize query latency, and write parameterized Cypher queries to uncover five core procurement fraud schemes.
The complete reference implementation is available in the fraud-detection-knowledge-graphs repository.
In accounts payable pipelines, risk checks typically operate on isolated records:
# Transaction-level view — nothing suspicious
transactions = [
{"vendor": "Alpha Corp", "amount": 5200.00, "date": "2025-08-01"},
{"vendor": "Beta LLC", "amount": 4800.00, "date": "2025-08-02"},
{"vendor": "Gamma Inc", "amount": 5100.00, "date": "2025-08-03"},
]
# All amounts within normal range ($1K–$15K). All vendors valid.
# Dates are sequential. Nothing triggers any rule.
When you map those same records to an interconnected graph, the hidden structure becomes clear right away:
# Graph view — all three vendors pay to the same account
connections = {
"ACC-MULE-001": ["Alpha Corp", "Beta LLC", "Gamma Inc"],
"ACC-0042": ["Delta Corp", "Epsilon LLC"],
"ACC-0099": ["Zeta GmbH"],
}
# ACC-MULE-001 receives from 25+ vendors. That's a money mule ring.
# The convergence is the red flag.
The underlying data hasn't changed. But when you evaluate transactions within an entity graph, the coordinated funnel stands out.
In a relational database, connecting these dots requires multiple joins across separate table. In a knowledge graph, the connections are stored directly as edges connecting nodes, which allows you to query them in a single traversal.
| Pattern | What It Is | What Traditional Tools Don't Catch |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate Invoices | Same invoice and vendor, near-identical amount, close dates | Exact match misses slight variations |
| Circular Rings | Vendors invoicing each other in a closed loop | Each invoice looks legitimate alone |
| Money Mule Rings | Many vendors funneling to one controlled account | No single payment is anomalous |
| Vendor Collusion | Independent-looking vendors sharing underlying attributes | No cluster detection across entities |
| Payment Anomalies | Invoice approved by someone outside their department's authority | Role-based checks pass, context checks don't exist |
A knowledge graph doesn't replace rules engines or ML models. But it does fill the gap they can't reach: relationships.

| Entity | Key Properties | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Vendor | tax_id, name, country, city | Who issues invoices |
| Invoice | invoice_id, amount, date, category | What was billed |
| Payment | payment_id, amount, date | What was paid |
| BankAccount | account_id, routing_number, bank_name | Where money went |
| Employee | employee_id, name, department | Who approved |
| Organization | org_id, name, departments | Structural hierarchy |
The base relationships form a bipartite payment network:
(Employee)-[:APPROVED]->(Payment)-[:LINKED_TO]->(Invoice)-[:ISSUED_BY]->(Vendor)

You likely use cloud services every day. When you check Gmail, join a Zoom meeting, or message your team on Slack, you use cloud-hosted software.
But you don't manage the servers it runs on or maintain the underlying infrastructure. You simply sign in and get to work. This is called Software as a Service (SaaS), and many people use it for years without knowing the term.
SaaS is just one of three major cloud service models. The other two, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and Platform as a Service (PaaS), give you different levels of control over the infrastructure and software you build. Understanding how these models differ will help you make sense of cloud engineering concepts and choose the right approach for your projects.
In this article, we'll break down IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, explain what you manage and what the cloud provider handles in each model, and learn how to choose between them for a real project.
By the end of this article, you'll be able to:
You don't need any cloud experience to follow this article. If you know what a computer, a server, and the internet are, you have everything you need.
If you're new to the cloud, read my article What is the Cloud and Cloud Computing? first. It explains what the cloud is and how it differs from running your own hardware, and this article builds on that foundation.
Cloud computing is a model that lets you use computing resources, such as servers, storage, and networking, on demand over the internet. YOu pay only for what you use.
These resources sit in data centres that are owned and run by cloud service providers, or CSPs for short. The best-known CSPs are Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.
This is just a short recap to make sure you understand the key concepts. My article above covers it in full if you want or need more info.
Before the cloud, most organisations ran their systems on-premises. On-premises means the hardware sits in a building the organisation owns or rents. This could be a server room in their office, with its own staff looking after it.
In this setup, you're responsible for everything. This includes buying servers, setting up the network, installing and updating software, and keeping the room powered and cool.
For example, if a small business wanted to launch an online shop, it would need to buy a server, install the software, and pay someone to keep it running. If the shop grew faster than expected, it would need to buy more hardware.
The cloud moves some of that work to the provider. The physical servers still exist, but someone else owns and maintains them, and you rent what you need.
What differs from one cloud service to the next is how much of the work the provider takes on for you. The cloud service models describe this, and there are three main ones:
So a cloud service model describes how the work is split between you, the customer, and the provider, that is which parts of the system you manage and which parts the provider manages for you.
The shared responsibility model defines which parts of a cloud system the provider manages and which parts you, as the customer, manage. To understand it, you first need to see the parts that make up a running application.
A computing stack is the set of layers that work together to run an application. Each layer depends on the ones beneath it. From the bottom up, we have:
AWS describes the split as security “of” the cloud and security “in” the cloud. The provider manages the security of the cloud. This covers the data centres, physical hardware, physical network, and the virtualisation layer.
But security in the cloud is the customer's job. It covers what you put into the cloud and how you configure it. This includes your data, your users and their permissions, and the settings of the services you use.
Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud model where the provider gives you the basic building blocks of computing. This includes virtual servers, storage, and networking.
With IaaS, you request a virtual machine from the provider. You choose how many CPUs and how much memory it has, which operating system it runs, and which network it connects to. Within minutes, the VM is running, and you can connect to it.
From that point, the server is yours to manage. You install your software, apply operating system updates, configure the firewall, and keep your application running.
Before IaaS, getting a new server meant ordering hardware and waiting weeks for installation. With IaaS, the same server is ready in minutes, and you can delete it when you no longer need it.
Just remember: IaaS removes the hardware burden, but it doesn't remove the server burden.
With IaaS, you usually pay for each hour or second a server is running, plus the storage you keep and outbound data transfer.

Marketing has always involved wrangling lots of data. Before digital marketing, businesses had to track sales, customer purchases, coupon redemptions, store traffic, and survey responses to understand what their customers wanted.
And while digital marketing didn't invent marketing analytics, it dramatically increased the amount of information out there.
Today, almost every interaction can produce data. A person might see an advertisement, click it, visit a website, read an article, subscribe to an email list, open several emails, add a product to a shopping cart, leave the website, return through a search engine, and eventually make a purchase. And every one of those interactions can potentially become a data point.
For a marketer, this creates an incredible opportunity. It also creates a problem: having more data doesn't automatically result in better decisions.
A company can have hundreds of thousands of customer records and still not know which customers are most valuable. A marketing team can have dozens of dashboards and still struggle to answer a simple question such as, "Which campaign should we invest more money into?"
This is where programming becomes useful. Python gives marketers a way to work with data programmatically. Instead of manually opening spreadsheets, copying formulas, filtering rows, and creating the same report every week, you can build reusable processes that perform those tasks automatically.
More importantly, Python allows you to go beyond simple reporting. You can use it to investigate customer behavior, discover patterns, perform statistical analysis, create predictive models, automate workflows, and build systems that continuously transform raw marketing data into useful information.

There's an important difference between learning Python and learning to use Python.
Learning Python means understanding syntax, data types, functions, loops, libraries, and other programming concepts. Using Python means taking those concepts and applying them to an actual problem.
This book focuses heavily on the second approach.

sources.title: How AI-Powered Search Works: A Guide for Devs on AI Visibility
sources.text:
Searched worked in a familiar way for decades: you'd type in your query, get back a list of pages, and choose one to click on. Behind the scenes, Google would find the pages it thought you might want, rank them, and give you a list of options.
But AI-powered search is changing that experience. If you ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, or another AI system a question, you may not get a long list of links to check out. Instead, the system can interpret your question, gather information from different sources when applicable, and generate an answer directly.
This changes something important for websites and brands: what happens when there's no traditional ranking position to fight for?
This is where the idea of AI visibility comes in. Instead of asking only, "Where does my website rank?", businesses and publishers are increasingly asking a different question: "Does the AI mention us when someone asks a relevant question?"
That distinction may sound small, but it represents a major change in how information is discovered online. And it's what we'll explore here.
If you're trying to understand how a search engine and an answer engine really work, it comes down to how each handles information retrieval.
Traditional search engines crawl the web, catalog pages in an index, run ranking algorithms against a user's keywords, and display candidate URLs ordered by perceived authority and link equity. The final decision of what to actually click on and read remains entirely in the hands of the person asking the question.
AI search changes things up a bit. When a user enters a natural-language prompt, the AI model decomposes the underlying intent, identifies candidate information using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (an AI technique that improves the accuracy of LLM models) or its pre-trained parametric memory, reconciles conflicting viewpoints, and actively decides which resources or solutions to present.
The most critical takeaway is that ranking highly on Google doesn't guarantee an AI engine will mention you. In fact, an Ahrefs citation study analyzing thousands of prompts discovered that only about 12% of URLs cited by generative assistants like ChatGPT and Copilot actually ranked in Google's top 10 for the exact query.
While Google’s own AI Overviews pull more frequently from conventional search results, standalone conversational engines construct independent answer graphs. AI visibility doesn't really care about claiming a specific URL slot. What matters more is whether your brand (and its resources) shows up as part of the machine’s direct answer.
If you strip away all the marketing language, AI visibility represents the probability and quality of your brand’s inclusion inside a synthesized response. Evaluating it requires breaking down three distinct dimensions:
This distinction matters because mentions and citations don't always happen together. An AI model can freely recommend your product because it understands your brand as a recognized entity, but cite a third-party tech review site as its primary factual reference. On the other hand, an engine might cite your documentation to clarify an API standard without ever suggesting your company as a vendor.
In order to appreciate how the AI chooses entities to include in its search results, we need to explore how modern retrieval engines work.
Current systems don't use only matching algorithms. They also incorporate elements of semantic analysis (the process by which an AI or computer program interprets the real meaning and context of words), vector representations (a way of turning words, sentences, or data into lists of numbers so that computers can understand their meaning) and multi-source verification (the practice of cross-checking a claim or dataset across multiple independent and reliable origins to confirm its truth and accuracy).
After the user provides the prompt, the system doesn't treat it as a set of words to be matched with an index. Using dense passage retrieval and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the engine translates the request into a high-dimensional vector embedding of the real semantic context. The system then searches candidate passages on the internet, analyzing them through a variety of signals:
Core Signal | What the Engine Evaluates | Why It Impacts the Response |
Semantic Relevance | Meaning, context, and vector proximity | Resolves the user's underlying intent rather than verbatim text. |
Information Density | Presence of hard data, statistics, and verifiable claims | Models favor text rich in concrete facts over vague qualitative descriptions. |
Attribution & Provenance | Citations and attributed external references | Transparent sourcing allows the model to ground its claims safely. |
Cross-Source Consensus | Corroboration across independent platforms | If independent review boards concur, models accept facts as the truth. |
Information Freshness | Recent timestamps and active updates | Ensures specs, pricing, and availability refl
